best_field_traits: INTRODUCED LANCEOLATE BROME: on the panicle find exceptionally LONG, narrow, pointed multi-flowered spikelets (typically ~25–50 mm) with EIGHT TO TWENTY florets. Measure spikelet body excluding awns; count florets and check lemma body ~12–18 mm under magnification. Do not mistake broad FLAT short-awn rescuegrass spikelets for the long narrowly tapering lanceolate form.
GENUS: Bromus PANICLES carry MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets; outer pair = GLUMES, inner overlapping units = LEMMAS, often with AWNS; not a true Hordeum/Elymus rachis SPIKE.
An annual, with lance-shaped many-flowered spikelets, usually longer than the short-flowered local bromes.
Many spikelets ~25–50 mm long and ~8–20 fertile florets (Kew GrassBase); some overlap Japanese and rescuegrass.
Lemmas typically ~12–18 mm, usually terminating in a small 2-fid/notched tip and one awn ~6–12 mm.
Check lower glume 3 veins versus upper glume 7–9 veins as confirmatory microscope details (Kew); photo macro presently missing.
Rescuegrass B. catharticus is COMPARISON ONLY: large BROAD FLATTENED spikelets with short or no awns; many awned bromes differ from it.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full plant and base to document annual habit
Entire panicle including all branch junctions
Close one long many-flowered 25–50 mm spikelet against mm ruler
Close glumes and fertile lemma teeth/awn insertion
True ligule, lower sheath and hair bases
crew_field_check: LOOK AT THE SPIKELET, NOT JUST THE DROOP: all four bromes have several florets stacked along one spikelet, often with lemma awns. First decide ANNUAL vs PERENNIAL, then count florets, measure the entire spikelet, individual lemma and awn, and inspect the glume veins and leaf sheath hairs. Nodding inflorescences or long awns alone are not a species ID.
Measure actual mature spikelet(s) with a millimeter ruler.
Inspect lemma/glume or true ligule ONLY where detailed pixels or a collected macro are actually available.
Record uncertain grass to genus, don't force the species from one photo.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).

field_matrix.where_to_look: At flowering inspect loose kinked/arching panicle BRANCHES; at fruit inspect lower/upper glume VEINS on intact source-verified spikelet.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair.
field_matrix.confirmation: Open macro: overlapping lemmas have long often twisted/recurving awns from below their apices; source descriptions vary considerably in spikelet length. Do not use a 10–15 mm cutoff to exclude Japanese brome.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Nodding and awns also occur in native Texas brome; compare intact mature glumes and source-labelled specimen.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Look at actual rooted crown, then hairy lemma surface at 10× and sheath/true collar.
field_matrix.look_alike: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma.
field_matrix.confirmation: A mature persistent perennial tuft/crown and hairy lemmas support pubescens, unlike short-lived Japanese, lanceolate and Texas annuals.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Hairy sheaths alone are NOT proof: multiple annual bromes have pubescent sheaths too. 389×589 archived source doesn't show lemma hairs.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Measure mature spikelet, glumes and lemma at mm scale; count veins on BOTH persistent GLUMES.
field_matrix.look_alike: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm.
field_matrix.confirmation: This 1/3 vein pair distinguishes from Japanese's commonly higher 3–5/7 vein counts. The lemma apex described as entire by FNA but sometimes toothed in other treatments: DO NOT force an ID from 'two teeth'.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: This is a botanically important native versus introduced split. Preserve TAXON/RANGE decisions and label uncertain lookalikes Bromus sp.; Hays County origin NOT proven from these photo references.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Inspect a mature INTACT glume pair and count actual longitudinal veins, not awns or background photos.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Whole flowering panicle: look for big FLAT, broad, oat-like spikelets with very SHORT or absent awns.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
field_matrix.confirmation: Large flattened overlapping V/oat-like florets contrast with Japanese brome's narrow long-awned units and lanceolate brome's narrower long densely floret spikelets.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Not installed in learner. Annual-versus-perennial is NOT sufficient: Texas A&M treats annual, Kew often perennial.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

not_reliable_alone: One awn length, purple seedhead color, or an overall nodding silhouette without attached spikelets.
Soft hair on lower SHEATH: found on multiple introduced and native Bromus species.
Whole head length alone: Flora of North America, Kew GrassBase and Texas regional treatments report overlapping but non-identical ranges.
Lower and upper glume vein count from a photograph that doesn't actually resolve the glumes under backlight.
Presence of yellow extruded ANTHERS: diagnostic of flowering grass stage, NOT Bromus texensis species.
An apparently perennial tuft when broken roots or mowing obscure annual/reproductive life cycle.
Unreviewed county nativity; rare native Texas brome may resemble introduced Japanese brome.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Introduced Mediterranean-region annual; check the LONG, narrow lance-shaped many-flowered spikelets (often roughly 25–50 mm) on an open branching panicle. For separation from other bromes, count florets and check the mature awn insertion and lemma-tip teeth with magnification.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalike_comparison: Introduced B. japonicus has slender, sometimes kinked/nodding panicle branches; its variable 15–40 mm reported spikelet lengths overlap other bromes. Native B. texensis has 1-veined lower and 3-veined upper glumes, 9–15 mm lemmas and straight 4–8 mm awns (FNA). Compare mature dissected spikelets. B. pubescens is a perennial of woodland understory with hairy lemmas and a loose drooping head; do not decide from habitat alone.

steps: 1 · GREEN TARGET: gallery 0, actual Dave Richardson panicle with green dense many-flowered spikelets; roots hidden.
2 · DRY TARGET: gallery 7, actual Yves Bas overlapping mature bracts, fine out-curving awns, bract-edge hairs; original source CC BY 4.0.

3 · ROOTED TEXAS VOUCHER: accession TEX-LL 00314236 under synonym Bromus macrostachys (collected Washington County in 1980) documents roots + flowering stems, but scan rights UNCONFIRMED: research citation ONLY, not a copied public photo.
4 · INNER COLLAR: lift true blade edge to show 1–2-mm membranous ligule and adjacent lower sheath hairs separately; no existing exact-species photo proves it.
5 · OPEN MATURE SPIKELET: expose two outer glumes, backlight their actual veins, include physical mm rule. FNA lower 3–5/upper 5–7; Kew gives lower 3/upper 7–9.
6 · LEMMA + AWN: detach fertile lemma and show two apical teeth and separate subapical awn insertion, do not assume the dense spikelet photo demonstrates exact boundaries.
7 · NATIVE COMPARISON: gallery panel 3 = B. texensis, 4 = B. pubescens; 1/2 both duplicate Japanese brome photo, 5/6 are rescuegrass.
8 · RELEASE ONLY after license, rooted plant, inner collar, measured glumes, independent source ID and live mobile annotation QA.

what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole rooted native-range flowering plant to document annual versus perennial duration and habitat.
Entire mature panicle including every branch origin and 2–3 intact ripe spikelets with 1 cm scale.
Paired lower and upper GLUMES opened without damage: count longitudinal veins using backlight at 10–20× and 1-mm ruler.
Mature lemma with measured length and actual terminal tooth/apex shape plus exact origin and length of single lemma awn.
Cross-section or profile of spikelet to document broad flattened rescuegrass versus more narrow lanceolate type.
Lower leaf sheath HAIRS and true membranous LIGULE at blade–sheath collar, photographed on same plant.
Compare a confirmed Texas brome against local Japanese brome under same 1-mm ruler before invasive removal.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — LONG LANCE-SHAPED SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Introduced annual; mature spikelets often 25–50 mm long with about 8–20 fertile florets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow the actual Dave Richardson green panicle (panel 0) from its short branches into densely crowded lance-shaped, multi-flowered spikelets. Then examine Yves Bas's dried spikelets (panel 7) with fine outcurving awns and bract edge hairs. Four additional CC BY Texas-source photos now provide a live Austin green head (panel 8), dry attached flowering culm (panel 9), and Burnet green mature spikelet (panel 10); panel 11 gives lower sheaths near soil. None shows extracted roots, a real millimeter scale, or separated glume nerves. FNA gives spikelets about 20–50 mm with 7–20 florets; count and measure on a source-authenticated mature specimen.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SIX SOURCE-LABELLED REAL PHOTOS: TWO ORIGINAL + FOUR TEXAS FIELD/REPRODUCTIVE, ROOT CROWN STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · ANNUAL ROOTS, SHEATH AND TRUE LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Verify an annual fibrous-rooted plant and the approximately 1–2 mm true membranous ligule.
field_id_short_tiles.details: FNA reports an annual with soft white hairs often on the leaf sheaths and a 1–2-mm obtuse or erose true ligule. GrassBase describes an eciliate membrane, so verify the actual free edge rather than assuming its fringe. New Texas panel 11 shows a true lower flowering culm and leaf/sheath exterior above soil, with actual roots hidden, and DOES NOT expose a calibrated inner ligule. The older two target photos showed only heads; sheath hairs remain unverified at macro scale. A Texas specimen under synonym Bromus macrostachys (TEX-LL 00314236, Cliff Morden 21, 27 April 1980, Washington County) DOES picture dried fibrous roots and flowering stems, but scan reuse rights have not been confirmed: it is a RESEARCH-ONLY lead, not a public gallery photo. Obtain licensed same-plant rooted base, flowering axis and true 1-mm-scaled ligule.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL LOWER SHOOT/SHEATH EXTERIOR PHOTOGRAPHED (PANEL 11); TRUE INNER LIGULE, ROOTED ANNUAL CROWN STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · BACKLIGHT THE TWO GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower glume commonly 3–5-veined; upper reported about 5–9-veined across treatments.
field_id_short_tiles.details: On ONE ripe target spikelet, separate both basal GLUMES and count their longitudinal veins by backlighting against a 1-mm ruler. FNA gives lower 3–5 and upper 5–7; Kew GrassBase generally gives lower 3 and upper 7–9. Those are published ranges, not measurements visible in panels 0, 7, or the newly archived Texas close green spikelet panel 10. For the native comparison, panel 3 is B. texensis, often 1-veined lower/3-veined upper; never mistake its photo for a laceolate brome organ.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TWO MEASURED BACKLIT GLUMES REQUIRED — TREATMENT VEIN RANGES DIFFER

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA BODY, TWO TIP TEETH AND AWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fertile lemma often 12–18 mm; awn approximately 6–12 mm, arising below the tip.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Yves Bas's dry macro (panel 7) shows true species-labelled overlapping pointed bracts, twisted/slender awns and fine edge hairs, not an independently detached lemma. FNA describes fertile lemmas about 11–20 mm and awns mostly 6–12 mm, sometimes longer. The added Texas close green spikelet (panel 10) shows overlapping pointed bracts and outward awns but not their anatomical insertion. Confirm the two short tip teeth and SUBAPICAL awn insertion on a separated floret with physical 1-mm scale. Do not arrow a crowded awn tip as a precisely assigned lemma origin without a visible continuous connection.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL BRACT PHOTO — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO DETACHED MEASURED LEMMA

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES — NATIVE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: Native Texas brome = panel 3; Japanese brome duplicate = panels 1 and 2
field_id_short_tiles.details: TARGET panels 0/7/8/9/10/11 are genuine B. lanceolatus, with four new CC BY Texas images. Panel 3 is NATIVE B. texensis, not panel 4. Panel 1 and panel 2 both point to the SAME Matt Lavin Japanese-brome JPEG, so they do not supply two independent comparison images. Panel 4 is native perennial hairy woodland brome B. pubescens; panels 5/6 are introduced broad-spikeleted rescuegrass B. catharticus. FNA lanceolate brome panicle branches are usually relatively rigid and shorter than the often 20–50-mm spikelets, as opposed to Japanese brome's often more flexuous panicle; appearances overlap, so confirm glumes and lemma before removal.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SIX GENUINE TARGET PHOTOS + LABELED COMPARISON BROMES; COMPARATIVE GLUME/LEMMA DISSECTION NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — TWO LANE HANDOFFS
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — crown, ligule and glumes remain
field_id_short_tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: real source-vouchered live annual rooted crown with attached flowering stem; hair distribution on lower sheaths; true membranous inner ligule 1–2 mm beside ruler; whole measured flowering head; two separated backlit glumes showing vein counts; mature isolated lemma and awn insertion, compared with B. texensis. NEEDS_SITE_QA: all six archived exact species photographs (four new Texas photos individually source-licensed), existing validated gross arrows, correction of the native Texas-brome comparison marker, duplicate Japanese comparison, mobile view and Pages build. Texas root-bearing herbarium voucher 00314236 is a rights-uncleared research lead ONLY. Four actual Texas species JPEGs installed in this pass; no new arrows, and no claims about microscopic glume or lemma anatomy.
